To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
lung function testing remains central to the diagnosis of CLAD and is influenced by a wide range of donor, recipient and surgery related factors.

1) lung function is an important biomarker in lung transplantation and 2) lung function is affected by a number of factors including the type of transplant, the age and the gender of the recipient and donor.
lung function testing in the lung transplant population is important to assess allograft function and to detect and diagnose CLAD.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the clinical application of lung function testing in adult and paediatric lung transplant recipients.
the development and validation of new biomarkers to improve our understanding of lung function following lung transplantation.
the clinical and molecular characterization of lung transplant rejection.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
lung function testing remains an essential component of routine clinical care of the lung transplant recipient.
spirometry remains a cornerstone in the follow‐up of lung transplant recipients.
spirometry remains the gold standard to assess lung function after lung transplantation.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
there are many factors that affect the lung function after transplantation, and that the maximal lung volume achieved is influenced by a variety of donor and recipient characteristics.
the interpretation of lung function testing is central to the diagnosis and prognosis of the failing lung transplant.
the lung allograft is a dynamic organ that undergoes continuous changes in its physiology following transplantation.
The main takeaway from our work is that
lung function testing remains the cornerstone in the evaluation of the transplanned lung.
lung function is an essential component of the clinical assessment of the lung allograft, and that it is influenced by a variety of donor, recipient and surgical factors.
lung function in lung transplant recipients needs to be interpreted within a broader context and that lung function alone is insufficient to diagnose the cause of CLAD.
